kurz: Why some companies defend their excess returns for decades, and how you can recognise this in the figures.

bloecke.md:
## How competition erodes excess returns

Capital flows to where it earns the most. This is why high returns are usually short-lived. A company that earns 25% on its capital employed in a market attracts imitators. Competition then pushes down prices, margins and ultimately the return on capital until it reaches the level of the cost of capital. Aggregated across all of the roughly 6,000 US companies, the return on invested capital ([[Return on invested capital (ROIC)|ROIC]]) in January 2026 was 10.1% after tax, and 9.0% after adjusting for leases and research expenses. The average cost of capital of the same companies was 7.0%. On a ten-year average, the return on capital was as low as 7.7%. The average company's lead over its cost of capital is therefore small, and the longer the measurement period, the smaller it becomes.

An **economic moat** explains why this convergence does not happen for a particular company, or at least happens much more slowly. The term refers to a structural reason why a competitor who sees the excess return and wants to attack cannot do so profitably. A good product, a strong quarter or a charismatic chief executive is not yet a moat. Warren Buffett popularised the image of the water-filled moat around a castle in his letters to shareholders. In economic terms, the question is how long ROIC stays above the cost of capital (WACC).

What matters most for a company's value is how long a high return on capital lasts, and less how high it is. Value is created solely from `(ROIC − WACC) × invested capital`, in every single year in which the difference remains positive. A company with 40% ROIC over three years is therefore worth less than one with 18% over thirty years.

## Six sources of economic moats

The common classification goes back to Michael Porter. Morningstar condensed it into five categories for equity analysis: intangible assets, switching costs, network effect, cost advantage and efficient scale. In practice, it makes sense to split intangible assets further into brand and rights granted by the state, because the two lose their protective effect in completely different ways. This gives six types. For each one, there is a test question that must be answerable in one sentence.

bloecke.md:
Two types are regularly confused. With **economies of scale**, fixed costs are spread over more units, so that the largest supplier produces most cheaply. This is a cost advantage that also works in large markets. **Efficient scale** describes the opposite case, a market that is too small for competition. A regional electricity grid operator, an airport, a pipeline or a rail network has no cost advantage in the strict sense. Its protection lies in the fact that a second supplier alongside it would make no sense. This moat is stable but only allows limited excess returns. Because it is obvious that a monopoly rent arises here, it is usually regulated and thus capped.

**Network effect** and size are not the same thing either. A food retailer only becomes bigger with its millionth customer, not better. A derivatives exchange is different. There, liquidity attracts more liquidity, because narrow spreads attract additional traders and their orders narrow the spreads further. One example is the Bund future. From 1988, it was traded mainly on London's LIFFE, until the electronic German derivatives exchange (Deutsche Terminbörse, now Eurex) won the majority in 1997/98 with lower fees. Within a few months, all trading then moved to Frankfurt, where it has remained ever since. An established contract is therefore protected for a long time, but once market share tips, the liquidity moves completely.

bloecke.unter: An economic moat is lasting protection against at least one of these five forces, all of which act on the achievable margin.

bloecke.md:
## Recognising economic moats in the figures

Qualitative descriptions of brands and networks are easy to write; the figures leave less room for manoeuvre. Three characteristics are meaningful:

1. The level of the return on capital above the cost of capital. If an industry's ROIC is permanently 20 percentage points above WACC, it has either an economic moat or a measurement problem.
2. The stability of the margin over a full business cycle. What counts is the worst figure of the last ten years, not the highest.
3. **Pricing power**, that is, the ability to pass on cost increases without losing volume.

bloecke.titel: Return on capital versus cost of capital by industry (US, January 2026)
bloecke.unter: After-tax return on invested capital, adjusted for leases and research expenses, compared with the average cost of capital of the same industry. Value is only created where the left bar is higher than the right one.

bloecke.md: The differences between industries are large. The tobacco industry earns around 56 percentage points above its cost of capital, the total market 2. The car industry is 7 points below and thus destroys capital overall. This can be explained with Porter's five forces. The tobacco industry has brands, regulated market access and a de facto advertising ban that hits newcomers. The car industry has powerful suppliers, powerful dealers, high fixed costs, aggressive new entrants and substitutes that extend as far as doing without a car altogether.

Research and marketing are booked as expenses and not capitalised. As a result, the most important asset of software, pharmaceutical and brand companies is missing from the balance sheet. Invested capital is therefore too small and ROIC correspondingly too high. If research expenses are counted as investment, the return on capital of the software industry falls from 54.3% to 29.3%, and that of the pharmaceutical industry from 32.7% to 17.0%. Both figures are still excellent. However, half of the apparent lead is due to accounting and not to an economic moat.

bloecke.md: The third measure, the ten-year average, is the most revealing. For tobacco, it is above the current unadjusted figure, for household products slightly below. In both industries, the return has been high and stable for a long time, with tobacco recently tending to decline. For software and semiconductors, the ten-year average is well below the current figure, so today's peak only emerged recently. Steel shows the typical pattern of a cyclical industry, with 6.9% currently and 20.9% on the ten-year average. An investor who, in a boom year, mistakes a steel company for a moat company because of its current return on capital is confusing a cycle with a structural advantage. The three columns are not methodologically identical, because the ten-year average is unadjusted. Even so, the comparison between the columns is meaningful.

Two companies each have €1,000 million of invested capital. Both reinvest so that their capital grows by 6% a year, and both start with a ROIC of 20%. The cost of capital is 8.5% in both cases. This is the average for the companies from Germany, Austria and Switzerland in the KPMG Cost of Capital Study 2025.

- Company A maintains its ROIC of 20%.
- Company B loses its lead evenly and is at 8.5% after ten years. Its return then equals the cost of capital and does not fall below it.

Undiscounted, the economic profits for years 0 to 15 add up to €2,952 million for A and €761 million for B. Company B is never a bad company at any point; it merely develops like an average one.

bloecke.md:
## Erosion of economic moats

No moat lasts by itself. Typical patterns of decay are:

- The distribution channel disappears while the product remains. For decades, classified ads were a very strong network effect for regional newspapers, because advertisers went where the readers were. The effect itself persisted, but it migrated to online platforms.
- The protective right expires. A European patent gives protection for 20 years from filing. For medicines, a supplementary protection certificate extends effective protection by up to five years. After that, the price of an originator drug falls within a few months. The expiry date is in the annual report and surprises nobody, yet many investors do not factor it in.
- The legislator opens up the market. The German telephone market was a state-protected monopoly until the end of 1997. After the market was fully opened on 1 January 1998, the price of long-distance calls fell sharply within a few years. Balance sheet ratios give no warning in such cases, because they remain excellent until the day of the change. The warning sign is in the official gazette, not in the accounts. The same pattern is repeating itself today with digital platforms, on which the EU's Digital Markets Act has imposed interoperability and switching options since 2024.
- An attacker changes the cost base. A cost advantage from a written-down plant looks very good on the balance sheet and disappears as soon as a competitor builds more cheaply with new technology.
- Management weakens the moat itself. Price increases beyond what customers consider fair, quality cuts at the same price or stretching a brand into unrelated categories increase the margin for three years, but at the expense of the moat.

bloecke.titel: Three quick tests for economic moats
bloecke.md:
1. Look at the return on capital as a ten-year series instead of a single year's figure, and within it pay attention to the worst figure, not the best.
2. Check the operating margin in a downturn year such as 2009 or 2020. An economic moat shows itself in a downturn and not in a boom.
3. Check whether the company has passed on cost increases without losing volume. If the whole industry raised prices at the same time, that proves nothing about the individual company.

A recognised economic moat says nothing about the price of the share. If a return of 30% over 20 years is already reflected in the share price, the moat is no longer worth anything to the buyer, because they pay for it in advance with the purchase price. Conversely, a company without a moat is not necessarily a bad investment if the market is pricing in only ten years of normal returns. Quality and valuation are two separate questions, and this lesson deals only with the first. None of this is a recommendation for individual securities.

mitnehmen: An economic moat is about the duration of an advantage, that is, how many years ROIC stays above WACC.
The average company earns barely more than its cost of capital, and on a ten-year average even less than in the current single year.
A large part of the high returns on capital in software, pharma and branded goods is an accounting effect, because research and marketing are not capitalised.
Growth is only valuable if the return on newly invested capital is above the cost of capital.
Moats protected by regulation can disappear without the figures giving any prior warning, because the warning sign is in the official gazette and not in the annual report.

begriffe.text: Structural reason why a company can permanently defend its return above the cost of capital against competitors. The duration of the lead matters more than its size.

Economic moat created by a narrow market. The market supports only one or two suppliers, and an attacker would make both unprofitable. Typical of networks, airports and pipelines, which are usually regulated and therefore have their returns capped.

Every additional participant increases the benefit of the offering for all existing ones. This must be distinguished from mere size, where additional customers bring only revenue and no additional benefit.
Cost in money, time, data and operational risk that a customer bears when changing supplier. Switching costs protect the existing supplier even when the competing product is objectively better.
Also called residual income or EVA, calculated as (ROIC minus WACC) times invested capital. A company creates economic value only from economic profit.
